# Nivāpa Sutta (MN 25 (PTS MN i 151))

**ID:** MN 25 (PTS MN i 151)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nivāpa Sutta* (MN 25) presents an elaborate parable in which the Buddha compares getting ensnared by Māra to herds of deer lured by fodder (*nivāpa*) laid out in a field by a sower or hunter (*nevāpika*) [Deleanu 2006; Pande 1974]. In the sutta's metaphorical schema, the crops or bait represent the five strands of sensual pleasures (*kāmaguṇa*), while the sower signifies Māra the Evil One [Deleanu 2006; Hazra 1994]. Three successive herds of deer succumb to the bait through greed and carelessness, whereas a fourth herd avoids the hunter's snares by establishing a dwelling out of reach, illustrating the progressive strategies required to overcome Māra [Deleanu 2006]. The spiritual path culminates in the sequential mastery of meditative absorptions, extending beyond the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*), whereby the practitioner completely blinds Māra and destroys the mental effluents (*āsavas*) [Yinshun; Li 2015].

Modern scholars have noted the close textual relationship between MN 25 and adjacent discourses. Govind Chandra Pande observes that the elaborate Nivāpa parable may represent an expanded composition built on shorter canonical comparisons, and highlights the shared subject matter and schematic account of meditative attainments connecting MN 25 to the *Pāsarāsi Sutta* (MN 26) [Pande 1974; Rogell 2003]. Yinshun notes that the Nivāpa Sutta explicitly places the concentration of cessation above the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a structural placement not universally shared across all Āgama lineages [Yinshun].

 DharmaNexus confirms alignment with this Chinese *Madhyamāgama* text and detects extensive internal Pali reuse across 117 texts [DharmaNexus]. In particular, the meditative attainment sequence (§§12.2–20.2) is nearly identical to MN 26 (§§34.4–42.3, similarity 0.99) and heavily shared with the *Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa* (Cnd 23) and *Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa* (Cnd 19), both of which cite the text [DharmaNexus]. Substantial overlaps in these meditative formula passages also occur in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 9 and AN 4) and Sanskrit texts such as the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* and *Daśottarasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
